  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

According to recent reports, in 1985, the W.M. Keck Foundation donated $70 million for the University of California and Caltech to construct a new observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The twin telescopes of the Keck Observatory would be larger than any previous telescope, and the first to use a segmented-mirror design. The goal was a facility that could see farther out into the universe, and with more detail, to study exoplanets, black holes, star and planet formation, and more.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 24, 1990, with only nine of the 36 segments of its mirror in place, Keck I turned skyward and achieved first light. The telescope’s image of NGC 1232 was an auspicious beginning of a long career for the Keck Observatory, furthered when Keck I was completed in 1992, and when Keck II was constructed and saw first light in October 1996. The twin telescopes would become the most scientifically productive optical and infrared telescopes in the world.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#180158. How This Creepy Critter Evolved Its Way to Surviving on Blood Alone

How This Creepy Critter Evolved Its Way to Surviving on Blood Alone

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood.
  • Recent findings suggest that because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals.
  • Evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood. But unlike the vampires of movies and folklore, they don’t drain their victims. These tiny creatures couldn’t possibly hold all the blood that’s inside the much larger mammals they feed on after dark. Still, they can still consume a seemingly supernatural amount because their stomachs are built to expand.

Recent findings suggest that because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals. When night falls, they fly out to forage, sometimes drinking up to half their own body weight in blood, thanks to those expandable stomachs and kidneys that rapidly get rid of excess fluid. The problem is that blood is a poor diet. It’s mostly water, with plenty of protein but potentially toxic levels of iron, and only traces of sugar and fat. Even so, it’s the only food vampire bats will ever know. Once the young of all three living species are weaned off milk, they switch entirely to blood. They start sinking their teeth into unsuspecting victims, mostly sleeping livestock, which feel little more than a mosquito bite.

Evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone. He and his research team set out to identify the changes in genes and gene expression that made this possible. They analyzed the genomes of the common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus), the hairy-legged vampire bat (Diphylla ecaudata) and the white-winged vampire bat (Diaemus youngi), and compared them with the genomes of other bat species. By analyzing gene expression in six major organs, including the stomach, they found several anomalies. Vampire bats’ stomachs were so different from those of other bats, and other animals, that they were almost a different organ entirely.

“Extreme dietary specializations impose strong and persistent selective pressures in nature, forcing organisms to reconcile severe nutritional imbalances with existing physiological and metabolic constraints,” Hiller and his colleagues wrote in a study recently posted to the preprint server bioRxiv. “Deciphering how genomes adapt to such conditions reveals general principles of the evolutionary processes that remodel metabolism and physiology.”.

Industry observers note that among the roughly 30,000 known tetrapod species, dependence on blood, known as obligate sanguivory, has evolved only once. Because blood offers so few calories for its volume, vampire bats have to drink large amounts of it. Because it also contains so little sugar, the bats have low baseline insulin levels and release little insulin after a meal. Some aspects of this metabolic situation resemble type 2 diabetes in humans, so studying these bats could lead to better treatments in the future. Much like fictional vampires, vampire bats also need to feed often. They have a very limited ability to store fat and glycogen, so they can starve if they go 48 to 72 hours without a blood meal. To prevent this, bats that have fed successfully sometimes regurgitate blood for roost mates that haven’t eaten that night.

In a recent development, the genomic shifts behind vampire bats’ sanguivory include changes in genes for digestion, metabolism and immunity, as well as the loss of bitter taste receptors. The vampire bat stomach in particular has adaptations found only in these three species. Its enlarged size is linked to three upregulated genes. These genes are also thought to play a role in the bats’ unusually shaped gastric glands and in extra connective tissue that makes such huge expansion possible. Most mammals use stomach acid to digest food, but vampire bats’ genes for producing gastric acid are suppressed. Digesting so much blood would take an enormous amount of acid, and the specialized mucus lining their stomachs leaves them vulnerable to acid damage. So over the course of their evolution, their stomachs shifted from digesting food to absorbing it.

Industry observers note that adaptations elsewhere in the body also help these winged vampires survive on their unusual diet. Insect-eating bats have an enzyme for digesting insect sugars that their vampire relatives lack. Vampire bats get hardly any sugar, so they have no need for it, which fits with their low insulin output. Vampire bats have also lost several genes that control gut movement in other species, but that matters little for an animal whose diet is a single liquid with little, if any, indigestible material. Similarly, having fewer fat-digesting enzymes is no disadvantage, since blood contains hardly any fat. Meanwhile, genes for coping with blood’s excess iron are enhanced. Vampire bats also rely more on their intestines to absorb amino acids and on their kidneys to reabsorb them, which keeps amino acids from being lost in urine.

Recent findings suggest that studying genomes and gene expression across several organs together was key to these findings. “This integrative approach was essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the molecular changes associated with sanguivory in vampire bats,” Hiller noted. “More generally, our work demonstrates how genome-wide, integrative analyses can yield molecular insights into the evolution of adaptive traits.”.

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside Latest York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marella Cruises‘ Discovery 2 is presently undergoing enhancements in a wet dock in Málaga, Spain.

According to a recent social media patch, the 1995-built vessel is being prepared to become an adults-only vessel, in addition to undergoing routine maintenance.

The former Legend of the Seas will undergo engine work and main pool retiling, with the Glass House Pool getting a fresh coat of paint and the atrium latest seating, complete with a refreshed Snack Shack.

The ship is set to welcome only adults starting in 2027 with former youth facilities transformed into four latest venues, including Marella’s first private karaoke lounge.

Amplify Karaoke will operate as a private lounge for up to seven guests, which can be booked by the hour.

Other new venues include the Lost Luggage Bureau, a speakeasy venue inspired by the Golden Age of Travel, allowing passengers to take part in two 90-minute shows that include live music, live actors, storytelling and three signature cocktails.

The Marella Discovery 2 will also introduce Red Handed, an escape room set backstage at the fictional Cabaret Rouge in the 1920s, where teams of up to six guests have 60 minutes to steal Lady Ruby Bardot’s diamond necklace before they’re caught red-handed.

Also being added is The Loft, which is described as a calm space for passengers who want to slow down, combining a library, board games, and hosted arts and crafts in a relaxed setting.

Following the enhancements in wet dock, the Marella Discovery 2 is scheduled to operate a winter season in the Canaries and Madeira, offering seven-night cruises from Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Puerto del Rosario to destinations in Spain and Portugal.

Latest Update: Astronomers catch ‘galaxy-killing’ wind in the act

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming latest stars.
  • Recent findings suggest that but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict.
  • Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the local universe, it is common to find galaxies that have stopped forming latest stars. These so-called quiescent galaxies have lived for billions of years and over that time, gradually exhausted their star-forming gas. By contrast, galaxies that lie at much greater distances — and thus appear to us when they were young, in the early universe — should have plenty of gas and be readily forming stars.

Recent findings suggest that but ever since it first began surveying the cosmos, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has discovered more quiescent galaxies within the cosmos’ first 2 billion years than current models of galaxy formation and evolution predict. Astronomers don’t know why they have stopped forming stars so soon, but they have many theories. Some of them require dark energy to have had a stronger influence in the early universe than previously thought, and thus have profound impacts on our understanding of the universe and its evolution.

Now, a team has found evidence that when galaxies collide — as they frequently did in the early universe — it can trigger a burst of star formation so intense that it generates winds capable of snuffing out the opportunity for any further stars to be born. This could explain the high number of young but unexpectedly quiescent galaxies JWST has found without needing drastic changes to our understanding of dark energy and its influence over time.

According to recent reports, in order to form stars, galaxies need reservoirs of gas that are dense and cold, lacking energy and prone to collapsing inward. One way to end a galaxy’s era of star formation — a process that astronomers call quenching — is to trigger strong winds that blast outward from the galaxy. These vast, high-speed flows of charged particles can blow away or heat this cold gas.

Recent findings suggest that such galactic winds can have two possible sources of energy. One is an actively accreting central supermassive black hole (called an active galactic nucleus, or AGN). The other is the energetic blasts generated by massive stars that form and then quickly die, ending their lives by exploding as supernovae. But astronomers have never caught such a wind in the act of draining its host of gas in the early universe, as it is difficult to get a detailed look inside a galaxy so far away.

To better discern the inner workings of star-forming galaxies in the early universe, researchers carried out a joint survey combining observations taken with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — a powerful radio observatory in Chile — and infrared data from JWST. They also turned to archival data from the Hubble Space Telescope. A team led by astrophysicist Rebecca Davies of Swinburne University of Technology in Australia spotted one particular galaxy, called CRISTAL-02, that shows what appears to be the first direct evidence of a wind powerful enough to halt star formation in a massive galaxy just 1.1 billion years after the Big Bang. The discovery was published June 10 in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

CRISTAL-02 is part of a larger sample of around two dozen star-forming galaxies at a similar distance (and therefore of a similar age). Observations showed a huge plume of cold gas extending outside the galaxy, almost as large as the galaxy it comes from. The plume is moving toward Earth at some 60 miles (100 kilometers) per second. Finding fast-moving gas so far from the galaxy is a sign the gas is being actively pushed out in a wind-driven process.

But to truly determine the nature of the plume, the team first had to rule out another possibility behind its formation: Because CRISTAL-02 also appears to be in the throes of merging with several other galaxies, the plume could be a tidal tail — gas stripped away by gravitational forces during the interaction, rather than a genuine wind. This was tricky to determine, Davies indicates, as no single measurement could settle the question of the gas’ origin; instead the team had to combine several different measurements to characterize the plume and confirm its cause.

First, Davies’ team measured how many upcoming stars the galaxy produces each year. Massive stars live much shorter lives than less massive ones, so looking at how many young, massive stars are in a galaxy indicates how promptly it is forming new stars to replace the ones that are dying. So, the team searched for signs of these young, massive stars in the galaxy’s spectrum and measured how bright those features appear.

In a recent development, the researchers also needed to determine how much gas the galaxy is losing. They did so by first using ALMA data to calculate the mass in the plume and then combining it with the gas’ velocity and distance from the galaxy’s center.

In a recent development, the verdict: CRISTAL-02 is forming stars at roughly three times the rate of a typical galaxy its size at this distance, but is losing twice as much gas as the galaxy’s star-formation rate. “If this rapid blowout continues, the galaxy could be dead in less than 50 million years, explaining the origin of the mysterious massive dead galaxies in the early universe,” Davies said in a press release.

According to recent reports, finally, the team turned to identifying the cause of the plume. Was the gas being pushed out by energy coming from the galaxy’s central black hole, or was the galaxy’s burst of intense star formation — and the resulting supernova blasts — the culprit?

In a recent development, models predict that the most powerful outflows from massive galaxies like these should be the result of accretion onto supermassive black holes, Davies notes. But CRISTAL-02 shows no sign of AGN activity in its center. On the other hand, based on the amount of massive young stars in the galaxy, Davies’ team calculated that the energy transferred to the surrounding gas as these stars die and explode as supernovae would be powerful enough to produce the observed plume.

It has been revealed that the speed of the gas backs this idea up. Supernova-driven outflows rarely exceed speeds of about 1,550 miles (2,500 km) per second, says Christy Tremonti, an astronomer at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the study. Velocities higher than this usually point to an AGN as the energy source. CRISTAL-02’s outflow is moving around 400 miles (640 km) per second, comfortably within the range expected for a wind produced by a powerful starburst.

According to recent reports, davies indicates that “the result is surprising,” going against the conventional wisdom that AGN are the cause of star-formation-ending winds. Tremonti notes that  “theoretical models love to use AGN feedback to shut off star formation in massive galaxies — almost every simulation does.” Yet CRISTAL-02’s star formation alone appears capable of triggering a wind that could exhaust its gas supply within tens of millions of years.

In a recent development, CRISTAL-02’s story may not be an isolated case, Davies states. Studies suggest that around 40% of massive star-forming galaxies in the early universe are merging, meaning many of them may be caught in similar growth spurts. If this commonly results in subsequent supernova-driven winds, it could help explain why so many early galaxies burned brightly and died young. “It may be the case that AGN are really notable for keeping star formation off, but maybe they’re not the thing that shuts it down initially,” Tremonti says.

Industry observers note that the case isn’t entirely closed. Davies notes her team cannot completely rule out the presence of an active supermassive black hole — either one too faint to detect, or one that may have flared briefly in the past and pushed gas away from the galaxy before subsequently fading from view. Tremonti agrees this is one of the hardest scenarios to eliminate. Future observations in the mid-infrared, which can peer through dust that might otherwise hide a buried black hole, could help close this gap.

As for CRISTAL-02, its fate is somewhat ironic: The explosive burst of star formation it is undergoing is also the underlying cause of its imminent death.

#180152. Phaethon’s fiery folly

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (388 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

Phaethon’s fiery folly

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even the best-laid prepares can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even the best-laid prepares can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

“There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” indicates Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

  • In a recent development, the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

In a recent development, the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

It has been revealed that the GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO stated Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

It has been revealed that white House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting fresh ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray said in a statement.

Industry observers note that sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters stated.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

Recent findings suggest that "I'm not a fan," said retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

It has been revealed that "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis stated. "Both are bad.".

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he mentioned the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman stated in a statement.

According to recent reports, ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

It has been revealed that before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Industry observers note that ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

It has been revealed that david M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

Gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

Recent findings suggest that deBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide currently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a fresh scale measuring masculinity.
  • For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health.
  • But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a fresh scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” notes Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

It has been revealed that those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

Sources indicate that the first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

Industry observers note that that thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

It has been revealed that inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”.

In a recent development, the higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” notes Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”.

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

In a recent development, englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

It has been revealed that he and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Recent findings suggest that but the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Industry observers note that then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their upcoming masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work highlights. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott notes. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”.

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott indicates. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”.

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he states. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”.

In a recent development, fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”.

Sources indicate that perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher indicates. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales right now in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

According to recent reports, below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

Movember Institute of Men’s Health.

According to recent reports, all the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher claims. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he states.

Sources indicate that A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”.

It has been revealed that researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, states psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a upcoming masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

It has been revealed that consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”.

Sources indicate that such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher states. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis states. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

Industry observers note that however the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”.

A-Rosa has entered a strategic partnership with Columbia blue to strengthen crew management and onboard hotel services across the European river cruise fleet.

Starting at the beginning of 2027, the Columbia signature brand will take responsibility for selected hotel crew recruitment administration and operational hotel services across the A-Rosa fleet operating on the Rhine, Danube, Rhône and Seine rivers.

The collaboration is designed to strengthen operational stability, broaden access to qualified personnel and support the long-term growth ambitions of A-Rosa, according to a press release.

Sources indicate that rolf-Dieter Maltzahn, CEO of A-Rosa, noted: “With Columbia blue, we are combining the brand and product expertise of A-Rosa with international recruitment and hospitality expertise. In this way, we are strengthening the continuous ability to offer our future guests the quality and personal travel experience that A-Rosa stands for.”.

Under the agreement, A-Rosa will retain its vertically integrated business model, including its own tour operator, shipping organization and fleet, maintaining full responsibility for strategic direction, brand positioning, product development, quality standards and the guest experience.

Columbia blue will complement this by providing specialist operational services, with A-Rosa remaining the framework for all onboard hotel operations.

“A-Rosa has a strong brand, a distinct product promise and extensive experience in the European river cruise market. We look forward to contributing our expertise and working together to develop an efficient and resilient model for hotel services,’’ noted Norman Schmiedl, CEO of Columbia blue.

The agreement comes as the increase in capacity, fresh market entrants and intensifying competition for experienced hospitality professionals across the European river cruise sector place greater demands on operators to secure skilled personnel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that the brain is a wondrous organ that’s so complex it’s often referred to as a computer, complete with electrical wiring in the forms of neurons, synapses, and axons. However, unlike computers, there’s no easy way to deftly repair faulty wiring, especially down at the cellular level. For decades, the best tools at a physician's disposal for tackling serious neurological diseases were medications or, in more dire scenarios, external therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

Those treatments can bring real relief, but they don’t fix the underlying problem. But if the brain really runs on electrical connections, shouldn’t it be possible to route signals around damaged areas by rewiring specific neurons? A team of U.S. researchers led by Kafui Dzirasa of Duke University School of Medicine thinks so. In May, they described a newly introduced technology called “LinCx” in the journal Nature. It uses engineered versions of proteins found in fish that naturally form electrical synapses, and it can link two specifically chosen neurons.

“For decades, neuroscience has lacked tools that can precisely control communication between specific cell types,” Dzirasa, the senior author of the study, remarked in a press statement. “By introducing a way to plug in newly introduced electrical connections with cellular‑level precision, our study marks a major step forward in the ability to edit brain circuitry and understand how neural networks give rise to behavior.”.

The system relies on structures called “gap junctions.” Each one is made of two hemichannels, and each hemichannel is built from six proteins called connexins. Through these gap junctions, cells exchange chemical and electrical signals, but they usually form unpredictably across cells. The innovation of the LinCx system is that it uses modified proteins that dock with one another while ignoring native brain proteins.

In a recent development, “The goal sounded almost simple: Make two proteins connect only to each other,” Carnegie Mellon’s Elizabeth Ransey, former Duke University postdoctoral researcher and lead author, remarked in a separate press statement. “We can specify both sides of the connection. That gives us much more precision than approaches that activate one population and indirectly affect everything downstream.”.

Sources indicate that the team tested the system in simple structures, such as human-derived cells and frog oocytes, and eventually moved on to more complex ones. Previous studies have rewired the neural circuits of Caenorhabditis elegans, a species of nematode commonly used in neurobiology. However, using the technology on mammals, specifically laboratory mice, was a first. In both worms and mice, the scientists noted changing behavior after performing this “neural bypass.” C. elegans, for example, modified its temperature-seeking behavior, and mice altered targeted responses to social interaction and stress.

By focusing on bypassing damaged areas rather than repairing them, physicians could provide improved brain function in those experiencing depression, autism, and many types of neurodegenerative disease.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Sources indicate that earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed.
  • In a recent development, this amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Jayne Hyde-Dryden was walking down a busy sidewalk along a noisy, two-lane road with her friend when she realized just how much her perception had changed. Mid-conversation, her friend interrupted and said, “Oh, that was fascinating. You just avoided a van without realizing you’d done it.”.

In a recent development, this amazed her friend because Hyde-Dryden is blind. She had used echolocation to detect the van, which was parked on the sidewalk, and navigated around it without even noticing. “I wasn’t consciously thinking about what I was doing at the time. Instead, I was naturally using echolocation, picking up changes in the way sound reflected from the vehicle and using that information to navigate around the obstacle,” claims Hyde-Dryden, a rehabilitation teacher in the UK. Like many blind echolocators, she creates a sharp, quick sound by clicking her tongue and then listens for the echo.

While echolocation comes easily to her now, Hyde-Dryden had to work hard to learn it. Almost 20 years ago, while she was losing her sight to glaucoma, she attended a short workshop and spent hours practicing the clicking technique she learned there. But she didn’t feel confident using it until 2019 when she signed up for an intensive echolocation study at Durham University.

That study was spearheaded by Lore Thaler, PhD, a neuroscientist at Durham University whose work over the last 15 years has uncovered how echolocation changes the brain. Her research goes beyond studying the variability of perception between people, and highlights just how much one person’s perceptual reality can change, even in a short timeframe.

Sources indicate that thaler started her research journey studying visual perception, but her work took an unexpected turn when a collaborator introduced her to a blind echolocator. At the time, she hadn’t heard of human echolocation, but “the way he described the world was very easy to relate to from a sighted person’s perspective,” she notes.

It has been revealed that after diving into the literature, Thaler found scattered and disjointed research on echolocation, and “very little was known about the brain basis of it,” she states. “That’s where we came in.”.

She and her collaborators used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to track two blind participants’ brain activity while they listened to recordings of their own echolocation clicks and echoes.

The auditory cortex responded more to echoes than non-echoes in both participants but so did regions of their visual cortex, including areas associated with visual shape perception. Even though this was what she had hoped to find, actually seeing it “was a wonderful surprise,” says Thaler, leading to “a great feeling of discovery.” When she and her team submitted the paper in 2011, the findings were contentious—so contentious that the journal they submitted to asked double the typical number of reviewers to take a look at it. Some thought it was an incredible finding; others thought it was predictable. But in the end, the paper got published, and when it did, it made a huge splash in the neuroscience community.

Industry observers note that the project shifted the way Thaler’s collaborators, and later many in the field, thought about the visual cortex. Perhaps the “visual cortex” was a misleading term, some experts thought. Instead, “maybe it’s a thing for processing spatial information,” claims Melvyn Goodale, PhD, a neuroscientist at Western University and Thaler’s collaborator on the project.

After that first study on echolocation, Thaler was hooked. She launched an entire lab of her own at Durham University dedicated to human echolocation research. She went on to study how echolocators perceive motion, navigate upcoming spaces, and distinguish between textures like velvet or glass.

By the time Hyde-Dryden made her way to Durham in 2019, Thaler was embarking on her most ambitious project yet: a 10-week echolocation training program for both blind and sighted people.

Each two-hour training session involved a slew of tasks. One involved standing in front of two foam discs and deciding which was larger. Another required participants to navigate through a virtual maze with recorded clicks and echoes. During every session, participants also explored an indoor or outdoor space with the help of Thaler or one of her collaborators to practice echolocating in the real world. Thaler even brought Hyde-Dryden to the Newcastle train station to help her learn the intricacies of echolocating in a busy, loud environment. Over time, Hyde-Dryden built up a mental “library of echo patterns” for familiar objects.

Both blind and sighted participants improved substantially at each of these tasks over the course of the 10 weeks. Just as in the initial 2011 paper and many of her follow-up studies, Thaler also wanted to understand brain activity during echolocation. This time, she had participants hop in the MRI machine both before and after learning to echolocate.

Industry observers note that before the study, Hyde-Dryden had heard from an expert blind echolocator that being inside of the MRI would feel tight and uncomfortable, but when she went into the MRI before the echolocation training, it didn’t bother her at all. After the training, however, the MRI felt quite different. “When I went in at the end, I felt horrendous. I felt ill afterwards. I felt really sick. And I think it was because I was more aware.”.

It has been revealed that those fMRI scans revealed that participants’ brains became attuned to echoes, whether or not they were blind. Echoes elicited a larger response in both the auditory cortex and in the primary visual cortex.

“It paired I think nicely with what we, up to that point, had only been able to show in these expert echolocators,” Thaler indicates. But it pushed the findings even further, demonstrating that participants don’t need to be blind to have malleable visual cortices. After just 10 weeks of training, the visual cortex becomes attuned to sounds that carry information about space. And other labs have shown that sighted people don’t even need to learn echolocation to retrain their visual cortex; a few days with a blindfold can tune your visual cortex to sound and touch signals it wouldn’t normally process.

In a recent development, since that training, Hyde-Dryden has started to use echolocation every day. “It really was an absolute game changer for me,” she states. Thanks to echolocation, when her daughter was young, Hyde-Dryden was able to use both hands to scoop her up from the bath, bringing her into the bedroom without having to hold a cane at the same time. In conjunction with her cane and guide dog, echolocation has made Hyde-Dryden feel much more confident navigating upcoming spaces. Even in busy train stations with high ceilings where the echo can get lost, she can find her way without assistance.

According to recent reports, despite success stories like hers, “it’s not a skill that is widely taught anywhere in the world,” Hyde-Dryden says. Echolocation is taught by a small number of people and is sometimes loosely included in rehabilitation curricula, “but it is certainly not given the emphasis that it should.”.

According to recent reports, thaler hopes to change that. She has offered free workshops for years and, this year, she prepares to give training sessions to more than 100 rehabilitation professionals at Guide Dogs UK who will then train their hundreds of clients.

Industry observers note that “I think the neuroscience stuff has been a good vehicle to drive home the message ‘this is real, this has to be taken seriously,’” says Thaler. “But then to actually go out and do the training and make it useful for people, of course, that’s still another step.”.

Nora Bradford is a cognitive scientist and science journalist. During her Ph.D., she investigated metacognition, or “thinking about thinking.” That research echoes throughout her science writing, as she typically covers perception, cognition, and learning across human and non-human animals. You can find her words in Scientific American, National Geographic, Quanta Magazine, and Science News, as well as in video-form on SciShow and PBS Terra. You can also visit her personal website at www.norabradford.com.

Windstar Cruises completed its third Mystery Cruise, an eight-night journey along Spain’s coast aboard the Star Legend.

Sailing from Barcelona to Málaga November 4–12, 2026, the voyage took travelers to a series of surprise destinations, giving them clues for each destination approximately 36 hours before arrival.

Beginning in Barcelona and concluding in Málaga, the eight-night sailing called at six ports: Mahón, Menorca; Castellón; Cartagena; Gibraltar; Motril; and Puerto Banús.

Windstar visited Castellón and Puerto Banús for the first time and returned to Motril after 18 years, having last called there in 2008.

“Our Mystery Cruises capture what Windstar is all about – a spirit of discovery, a sense of adventure, and the opportunity to experience the world in unexpected ways,” stated Chris Prelog, president of Windstar Cruises.

According to recent reports, “There’s something special about stepping aboard without knowing exactly where the journey will take you and trusting that incredible experiences await. The enthusiasm we’ve seen for these sailings has been remarkable, and we’re excited to continue bringing this unique concept to new destinations around the world.”.

Throughout the voyage, guests had the opportunity to experience the destinations through shore excursions showcasing the region’s history, culture and gastronomy.

Experiences ranged from coastal hiking adventures and explorations of historic fortresses to visits to local wineries, villages and regional culinary experiences.

As previously reported by Cruise Industry News, two additional Mystery Cruises are planned for 2027: the Northern Europe Mystery Cruise aboard the Star Pride and the Japan Mystery Cruises aboard the Star Seeker.

Newly introduced aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov.
  • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
  • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune said of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

According to recent reports, “They got to give us an update,” Tillis remarked. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

According to recent reports, the White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy stated the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand new architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy mentioned on CNBC Monday. “This can happen quickly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

Recent findings suggest that A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he said included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune remarked Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the newly introduced request specifically for air traffic control related problems, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

According to recent reports, “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune stated. “We’ll hear him out.”.

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the upcoming funding request.

Sources indicate that “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., said on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#180142. Breaking: Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

Breaking: Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20.
  • By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Emily Conover and Kathryn Hulick.

Recent findings suggest that A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Recent findings suggest that now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge stated he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

Recent findings suggest that A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” notes Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

It has been revealed that the result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono notes. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”.

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Industry observers note that alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”.

Recent findings suggest that AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”.

Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra indicates. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transcend Cruises has launched its inaugural CEO-in-Residence Program, where its CEO Edie Rodriguez will spend a month sailing the Rhine onboard the Transcend Connect.

As a newly appointed CEO and board member, Rodriguez will run daily executive operations and leadership meetings from the ship between November 23 and December 22, 2026.

In what is remarked to be the first time a cruise line CEO has spent an entire month onboard on either a river or cruise vessel, Rodriguez will meet with the onboard crew, charter clients and their guests and partners to help evolve Transcend’s brand strategy and product offering.

Corporate charters, MICE planners, travel advisors and affinity groups will also be able to connect and discuss customized itineraries and onboard experiences.

“Transcend Cruises was created to reimagine how groups come together on the rivers of Europe, turning every vessel into a customizable floating venue,” said Rodriguez.

“Setting up my office onboard for a month allows me stay close to our crew and operations and collaborate directly with clients and partners, and to experience the journeys just as they do and to better understand areas where we can improve as we continue to grow.”.

As the first charter-only river cruise manufacturer with ships built exclusively for the group, Transcend welcomed its first ship, the Connect this summer, embarking on its first voyage on August 3, 2026.

Two additional ships are currently under construction, with plans for the fleet to reach four in 2028 and ultimately grow to 12 ships.

The Azamara Quest is currently wrapping up a drydock in Elefsis to become the first ship to undergo refurbishment as part of the Azamara Forward program.

After wrapping up its summer season in Piraeus, the vessel arrived at a Greek shipyard on October 31, 2026.

As part of the project, the 2000-built ship is getting a newly introduced deck with more staterooms, in addition to refreshed public rooms, as well as new venues, such as the Atlas Bar.

All staterooms are also being updated with upcoming finishes, improved lighting and design details aimed at enhancing comfort.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced Penthouse Deck adds 12 additional suites. The new premium staterooms will also introduce two new suite categories to the firm’s fleet: Panorama and Grandview.

“We have designed these suites to have that calming, welcoming environment of a home away from home feeling for our guests,” said Martha Brabham, vice president of design and revitalization.

“So we would love our guests to enjoy the color scheme, the palette. We curated the elements in the room to really immerse you into that ocean experience.”.

Upon completion of the enhancements, the Azamara Quest is now scheduled to welcome guests back on November 26, 2026.

The ship is then set to offer itineraries in the Mediterranean, the Atlantic and the Caribbean before kicking off Azamara’s annual World Cruise in 2027.

“As the ship undergoes drydock, there’s a lot of work happening behind the scenes to bring Azamara Forward to life,” Azamara remarked in a status update.

“From refreshed spaces to thoughtful enhancements throughout the ship, every detail is coming together as the transformation takes shape,” the company added.

All ships in the manufacturer’s fleet are scheduled to undergo refurbishments as part of the Azamara Forward program.

The Azamara Onward will undergo the refit next, entering drydock in late 2027, followed by the Azamara Journey in late 2028.

Eagles can prey on adult baboons. Did our ancestors face that threat?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation.
  • According to recent reports, biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

As if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.

According to recent reports, biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).

Industry observers note that researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as big cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.

“It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” states Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.

Three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.

While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter says.

“I found the evidence pretty compelling,” says Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.

According to recent reports, the eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter says. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.

While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.

When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter indicates.

It has been revealed that the eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter notes. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.

Sources indicate that the threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.

“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really crucial precursor [of language],” Hobaiter says.
