    How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions.
    • Recent findings suggest that I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive.
    • You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

    You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

    You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

    Historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

    According to recent reports, from the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

    A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

    Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

    The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    After a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

    Back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

    In a recent development, close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

    In a recent development, A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

    For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

    Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

    Day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

    According to recent reports, the delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

    Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

    It has been revealed that or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

    Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

    The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

    According to recent reports, A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

    These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

    You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

    Industry observers note that naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

    Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

    For a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

    #180037. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (771 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
    • In a recent development, former Rep.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    In a recent development, former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    Recent findings suggest that the Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola stated in a statement after the race was called.

    Industry observers note that the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    Recent findings suggest that but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

    Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    According to recent reports, the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    In a recent development, "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer mentioned in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    The Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hoping to discover some of the best places to go in Europe in 2027?
    • According to recent reports, we’ve asked our expert contributors from all around the globe to nominate the spots that are on the up—the places that are on their radar thanks to a flock of hotel openings, major cultural moments, talk of fresh flight routes, or concerted conservation efforts taking root.
    • In a recent development, from untamed wilderness in the Albanian Alps to the world’s oldest art fair (celebrating a massive birthday in 2027) in Cologne, off to everyone’s latest favorite coastal coolcation destination in Denmark, this is our guide to the latest and greatest in Europe in 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hoping to discover some of the best places to go in Europe in 2027? No wonder: 2026 was a bumper year for European travel, from the Winter Olympics fueling a surging obsession with the Dolomites to the total solar eclipse bringing hoards of umbraphiles to the Balearic Islands, and celebrity weddings adding to an ever-growing love for Sicily. But as we edge closer to the end of the year, there are a few clear-cut destinations we’re most looking forward to visiting (and recommending to you, our fellow travelers) for the 12 months to come.

    According to recent reports, we’ve asked our expert contributors from all around the globe to nominate the spots that are on the up—the places that are on their radar thanks to a flock of hotel openings, major cultural moments, talk of fresh flight routes, or concerted conservation efforts taking root. These nominations make up the Best Places to Go in Europe in 2027—and we promise they are worthy of your precious vacation time and hard-earned spending money.

    In a recent development, from untamed wilderness in the Albanian Alps to the world’s oldest art fair (celebrating a massive birthday in 2027) in Cologne, off to everyone’s latest favorite coastal coolcation destination in Denmark, this is our guide to the latest and greatest in Europe in 2027. Happy travels. —Olivia Morelli.

    This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

    Go for: untamed wilderness and peaceful pockets.

    The Albanian Alp's village of Theth is a patch of pastoral living—and fantastic hiking trails.

    Local bed-and-breakfasts and guesthouses welcome trekkers, who do both day treks and through hikes connecting small towns.

    According to recent reports, as Albania’s allure continues to grow, travelers flock to the Adriatic beaches of the south. But in the northern alpine region, the scenery offers a different type of drama—jagged snow-dipped peaks, turquoise rivers, hut-to-hut hiking—and in place of shiny seaside hotels, Albanian-owned wooden B&Bs welcome alpinists for home-cooked meals after long, satisfying days on the many surrounding trails. This area was largely isolated during the communist era, given its strategic location along the borders with Montenegro and Kosovo, which means that it has been slower to open its arms to the world (that’s also why you’ll stumble into countless abandoned bunkers from this period on your hike). The feeling here is that you can still show up to a guesthouse without a reservation, you can still camp wherever you find a spot, and, yet, there is also the sense that if you aren’t seeing this place now, or within the next couple years, you’ll miss the precious moment when it still feels like a secret to be let in on.

    According to recent reports, start your trip in the charming city of Shköder, known as the gateway to the Alps, where bikepackers cycle through the city, and restaurant patios spill over with guests enjoying glasses of Albanian wine. From there, many travelers blueprint stops in the villages of Theth and Valbona (a stunningly scenic one-day through-hike links the two of them), or embark on ambitious multi-day journeys on routes like the Peak of the Balkans, which traces a two-week-long loop crossing into Kosovo and Montenegro. Infrastructure improvements have made roads and trails to access this region better in recent years, with much more where that came from. What was once only known by residents and those who purchased their paper guides now exists online, meaning it is also possible to base yourself in, say, the Eden-like Valbona Valley, and embark on a newly introduced route each day. Increasingly, there are elevated places to stay that preserve the soul of this place, opening in a slow trickle like Valbona Resort and Spa (2024) and SeSam Villas in Theth (2025). There may be folklore calling these the Accursed Mountains, but only because they are so vast and dramatic that their geography has historically kept intruders out. For hikers, that means a literal playground, with Albanian hosts leading the way. —Megan Spurrell.

    Go for: the next World Expo centered on play, and a booming hotel scene to match.

    Belgrade is set to host the World Expo in summer 2027, and a flock of fresh hotels will be ready to receive the travelers it is sure to bring.

    It has been revealed that all the world’s coming to Belgrade next year—and, it seems, coming to play. The Balkan city will host the next edition of the World Expo, a spiritual successor to the World Fair where nations come to exchange their latest and greatest cultural achievements and boldest ideas for the future. From May 15 to August 15, 2027, Belgrade plans to welcome over four million visitors to explore the theme of “Play for Humanity: Sport and Music for All." Its status as a host city feels especially symbolic as the Balkans emerge as a leader in technology and innovation across Europe. To meet the occasion, the city’s hotel scene is stepping up, with 15 latest openings slated to cut the ribbon by the time the program kicks off. The crown jewel in the portfolio is the Ritz-Carlton, Belgrade, which will occupy a prime spot on the Danube riverfront. Other big names to watch out for include the InterContinental Belgrade and the Swissôtel Belgrade. In total, these projects will add roughly 1,500 to 2,000 new hotel rooms to the city. The shiny, new threads go well with the old in a place as historic as the Serbian capital, which lays claim to grand sites such as the Church of St. Sava, one of the largest Orthodox churches in the world, and the Museum of Yugoslavia, which has a sprawling eight-acre park complex. —Kat Chen.

    Go for: a coveted summer destination at its sweet spot.

    A slew of luxury openings like Aman and Mandarin Oriental have arrived in Bodrum over the past few years, with NG Sign Bodrum and Bvlgari on the horizon.

    For the past few summers, the glittering Bodrum peninsula has welcomed a wave of luxury openings, transforming this once-sleepy harbor town into one of the Aegean's most coveted corners. Aman, Mandarin Oriental, and homegrown Maçakizi were early champions of the scene and remain firmly at the heart of its appeal, but a new generation of hotels, restaurants, and beach clubs has since made Bodrum one of Europe’s most sought-after summer escapes.

    Sources indicate that mayfair and Knightsbridge restaurant favorites Zuma, Bagatelle, and Novikov have all made the journey east in recent years, accompanied in 2026 by oh-so-chic arrivals from Dubai, Paris, and Marbella (Gaia, Gigi Rigolatto, and Maison Revka). Together they have helped recast Bodrum as a playground for the international jet set, bringing with them a distinctly cosmopolitan, see-and-be-seen energy.

    This summer also brought the long-awaited arrival of the adults-only hideaway Oku, the latest in the brand's collection of design-led retreats in Ibiza, Kos, and Andalusia. Throw in annual beach-club takeovers from the likes of Jacquemus and Alo, as well as boutique openings by brands like Cartier, and it seems there’s barely a name in luxury that isn’t lining up to plant its flag here.

    According to recent reports, but 2027 promises to be the sweet spot. With fewer headline-grabbing releases, the peninsula settles into a quieter rhythm, and openings such as Yahşi Bay’s NG Sign Bodrum, a villa hotel of sun-filled, glass-walled residences with two to six bedrooms, put privacy ahead of spectacle. It's the summer to explore Bodrum at its most relaxed. Reservations are likely to be easier to come by as last year’s hottest tables settle in for the latest season and the eyes of trend followers will be trained elsewhere, leaving the regulars to do what they’ve always done: Dance as the sun sets on the wooden deck of Maçakizi, wander the meyhane-lined promenade of fishing village Gümüşlük, stopping for fresh seafood as they go; or hop between the coastline’s secluded bays, tucking into late-afternoon picnics beneath the pine trees.

    Recent findings suggest that enjoy it while it lasts. In 2028, all eyes will return to the peninsula as Bvlgari opens its sprawling hillside resort above yacht-speckled Paradise Bay, giving Europe's luxury travel crowd fresh reason to return. —Sophie Prideaux.

    Go for: Irish hospitality and spectacular sporting scenes.

    The 46th Ryder Cup will take place at Adare Manor in County Limerick.

    Designed by golf course architect Tom Fazio, Adare is nestled upon 840 acres of parkland.

    It has been revealed that home to natural wonders, ancient castles, lively pubs, and famously friendly locals, Ireland has long captivated travelers. While the well-trodden tourist trail takes in perennial favorites, 2027 will see another destination step into the spotlight. County Limerick, on the west coast, is gearing up to host one of the world’s greatest sporting events: the 46th Ryder Cup. Between September 17 and 19, the tournament will take place on the pristine fairways of the prestigious golfing estate Adare Manor. Designed by renowned golf course architect Tom Fazio, the championship course is set within 840 acres of magnificent parkland surrounding the estate’s 19th-century Neo-Gothic castle—a fairytale destination worth visiting at any time of year.

    It has been revealed that beyond golf, Limerick has a rich sporting heritage. Thomond Park, home of Munster Rugby, is one of the best-supported grounds in the world, with match days bringing a buzz to the city. Beyond the sporting calendar, there’s plenty to discover. Highlights include the 13th-century King John’s Castle, the Hunt Museum for its art collection including works by Picasso and Renoir, and Lough Gur, an idyllic lake beside Ireland’s oldest and largest stone circle. Limerick also makes an excellent base for exploring the Wild Atlantic Way. Around an hour northwest of the city, Lahinch is widely regarded as one of Ireland’s best surf beaches, while the spectacular Cliffs of Moher rank among the country’s most beloved landmarks. With world-class golf, a proud sporting heritage, fascinating history, and easy access to some of Ireland’s most spectacular scenery, Limerick is set to have its moment in 2027. —Camilla Hewitt.

    Go for: a city break that’ll stay with you long after you’ve left.

    In Cologne's Old Town, the charm is in the details, like this whale lantern outside Brauhaus Sünner im Walfisch .

    If you visit for Cologne's exuberant carnival, say as the locals say: “Morje es, wat do drus mähs!” (“Tomorrow is what you make of it!”).

    Let’s be honest: Cologne doesn’t necessarily win you over at first sight. It is not a conventionally beautiful city; rather, it is a feeling. Even locals will tell you that the city gets under your skin. Anyone who has experienced Cologne’s exuberant carnival spilling onto its streets and into its clubs and pubs is likely to fall for the city—and its people—for good. The motto for the so-called fifth season in 2027 is “morje es, wat do drus mähs!” (“tomorrow is what you make of it!”). Multiple crises or not, the people of Cologne refuse to let anything dampen their spirits.

    Sources indicate that and while folk culture is a major part of Cologne’s appeal, the city’s high culture is equally compelling. In September 2026, the opera house on Offenbachplatz finally reopened after 15 years of renovation—an occasion eagerly anticipated by many. Just 160 yards away is Kolumba, the museum designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect Peter Zumthor. Its lofty, lime-washed rooms and the gentle light filtering through the narrow gaps between walls and floor provide a quietly dramatic setting for the art—and a welcome respite from the bustle of the city. Zumthor built the museum around the ruins of the former St. Kolumba church, incorporating the Madonna in the Ruins chapel by Gottfried Böhm. The work of two exceptional architects brought together in one place: that alone is reason enough to come.

    The Museum Ludwig is another perennial draw. In 2026, it recorded its highest-ever visitor numbers thanks to its exhibition devoted to the late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama. Art, in Cologne, is very much a capital-A affair. Every autumn, the international art world descends on the city for Art Cologne, the world’s oldest contemporary art fair, which celebrates its 60th anniversary in 2027. The 200th anniversary of Beethoven’s death is being marked in equally spectacular fashion. Throughout the year, the Cologne Symphony Orchestra will welcome a stellar line-up of renowned conductors and ensembles. The musical celebrations culminate in October, when pianist Igor Levit will take on all 32 of the great composer’s piano sonatas in a single evening.

    Sources indicate that the city’s famously warm and open-hearted inhabitants are just as welcoming when it comes to gastronomic newcomers. Julia Komp, who became Germany’s youngest Michelin-starred chef in 2016 at the age of 27, knows this well. Today, her restaurant Sahila is firmly at the forefront of Cologne’s culinary scene. Other top tables include the intimate 20-seat Onda on Händelstrasse; Vunky on Eigelstein, specializing in plant-based fine dining; Toki, the city’s first kaiseki restaurant; and the recently opened Kluth, whose six-course surprise menu, “et kütt wie et kütt” (“it is what it is”), takes its name from a quintessential Cologne saying. —Ilona Marx.

    Go for: rugged landscapes and cinematic coastlines.

    Sailing yacht Orient Express Corinthian's itineraries will set sail to Bonifacio, Calvi, and Saint-Florent in 2027.

    Hotel Basgi Basgi is a favorite among design lovers in Corsica—a grow that is increasingly looking to the island.

    When Simon Jacquemus chose Phare de la Pietra, a 19th-century lighthouse on a rocky Corsican peninsula, as the backdrop for his Spring 2027 fashion show this summer, it was easy to see why. The designer, long inspired by the interplay of place, light, and raw emotion, described his show Le Bonheur (meaning “happiness” or “bliss”) as “a cliff that I add colors on top. An impressionist painting.”.

    It has been revealed that it's true. Corsica is a place where cinematic elegance meets rugged natural beauty. It's why the island was once named Kallisté, meaning “most beautiful,” by the ancient Greeks. Here, dramatic mountains meet wild hinterlands and fiery red rockfaces jut against turquoise waters, making for breathtaking hiking through UNESCO-listed landscapes such as the Scandola Nature Reserve.

    In a recent development, the island long slipped under the radar compared with neighboring Sardinia and the French Riviera. But Jacquemus’ arrival, coupled with a flurry of recent smart hotel openings, suggests that may not be the case for much longer. Leading the charge is A Mandria di Murtoli, a 10-room retreat spread across five restored stone buildings in the Ortolo Valley, which is a little sister to epicurean Domaine de Murtoli, where farm-to-table living is the order of the day. Elsewhere, Hotel Mylos on the west coast and Basgi Basgi in the north are drawing an increasingly design-conscious crowd.

    Adding to the island’s momentum is the maiden voyage of the Orient Express Corinthian, a sailing yacht with 2027 itineraries calling at Bonifacio, Calvi, and Saint-Florent, opening up Corsica's fishing ports, medieval citadels, and spectacular coastline to a fresh wave of travelers. —Ashleigh Spiliopoulou.

    Go for: a coolcation destination with Michelin status.

    Newly-opened Betty Beach brings street food and brewery offerings to the beachfront of the Danish Riviera.

    The 60-mile so-called Danish Rivera is dotted with fishing villages, seaside resorts, and beaches.

    With rising summer temperatures across Europe, the Danish Riviera has emerged as the continent's favorite coastal coolcation destination. This 60-mile coastal stretch in Northern Zealand brings travelers the aesthetic appeal and culinary credibility of Copenhagen, but in a relaxed setting of fishing villages, sandy beaches, forests, and historical seaside resorts that remain largely undiscovered by international visitors.

    The Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Humlebæk marks the southern end of the riviera, but many visitors staying in Copenhagen don't venture any further north to seaside towns. Many of the region's charming seaside hotels date back to the late 19th century. But a new generation of stays is rejuvenating the landscape with contemporary design. Cori in Hornbæk brings barefoot energy to a beautifully repurposed former hospital, and Hôtel de Ville in Gilleleje transforms an old town hall into an eclectic boutique spa hotel.

    Exceptional gastronomy abounds, with Michelin-starred standouts such as Jordnær, The Samuel, and Parsley Salon representing New Nordic Cuisine at its finest. For something more casual, recently opened Betty Beach combines beachfront dining, street food, and a brewery for sun-kissed imbibing. Denmark's first official wine route launched last year in North Zealand and Odsherred, with nine wineries offering tours and tastings of cold-climate grape varietals such as Solaris and Rondo. —Amber Gibson.

    Go for: wild Austen-esque adventures and spa stays galore.

    Dartmoor's vast landscape, made of granite tors, walking paths, and moorland, brings the drama of Sense and Sensibility to life.

    In a recent development, dartmoor has always lent itself to drama. Wild ponies pick their way through heather, granite tors loom out of the mist, and the ever-changing weather plays a starring role. Now it’s getting its close-up as the backdrop of Georgia Oakley’s newly introduced Sense and Sensibility adaptation in theaters in September 2026. The film was shot around Princetown, Tavistock, and Gutter Tor, and its release coincides with Dartmoor National Park’s 75th anniversary. As the Austen connection pulls focus to Dartmoor, 2027 is the year to stay a little longer and explore a little further.

    In a recent development, it’s unusually special in the depths of winter, when the weather gets wild. Picture misty mornings walking the ancient tracks and climbing tors, and afternoons yomping across moorland in conditions that demand retreating somewhere cozy for a hot bath and a roaring fire. For a hands-on experience, book one of the free conservation days running on selected Sundays in 2027 to learn more about Dartmoor’s prehistoric archaeology, wildlife, and rare species while helping to preserve its future. Don’t miss Tavistock, the old market town on Dartmoor’s western edge. Its handsome Pannier Market is bursting with antiques and curiosities, ideal for a spot of treasure hunting. For a change of pace, visit 11th-century Buckfast Abbey, where the Benedictine monks still make their famous tonic wine to a secret recipe.

    Sources indicate that to feel like a main character in your own period drama, book a room at Boringdon Hall. This show-stopping historical hotel on the edge of the moor combines roaring fires and old-world grandeur with one of Devon’s best spas. Its Michelin-starred Àclèaf restaurant retained its star in 2026, a quietly heroic achievement in a world obsessed with shiny new openings. There is nothing like spending the wildest part of the year getting wind-beaten on Dartmoor, then retreating for a spa treatment, proper grub, and a fire. —Zoe Cook.

    Go for: a hidden culture hotspot on the Iberian Peninsula.

    Évora, Portugal's prettiest city, is now home to the Vermelho by Christian Louboutin hotel.

    Évora's artisan traditions that helped earn the city its title as a European Capital of Culture.

    According to recent reports, although there’s really no need to do so—Évora is impressive in its own right—we sometimes refer to this little historic city as the Seville of Portugal. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986, its center comprises an imposing Roman temple, known as the Temple of Diana; a Gothic cathedral; the eerie Baroque Cathedral of Bones, next to the Church of St. Francis; and the Renaissance Palace of King Manuel I.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2027, Évora will turn even more heads as one of the European Capitals of Culture. But Portugal’s prettiest city remains, overwhelmingly, a peaceful place, where at many times of the year you can stroll around in near silence. Then there’s the food. Restaurants such as Tua Madre, A Cozinha do Paço, and Forno da Telha allow you to discover recipes deeply rooted in the land and tradition. Don’t leave without trying porco à alentejana (clams and pork stew), ensopado de borrego (lamb stew), and a variety of local soups. And bread—plenty of bread—with superb olive oil. There’s also wine, of course, produced on the herdades (traditional estates dotted throughout the Alentejo region). After so much eating, you’ll need to get out and about. Which is perhaps why we find the concept behind Évora’s status as a European Capital of Culture so charming—the motto is based on the Alentejo’s cultural way of being: vagar, or to wander. —David Moralejo.

    Fuerteventura's volcanic landscape offers a stirring contrast to its surf beaches—and a unique draw for travelers headed to the Canary Islands.

    Boutique stay Casa Montelongo is one of several design-forward gems, this one tucked away in the charming village of La Oliva.

    The second-largest and oldest of the Canary Islands, Fuerteventura is promptly establishing itself as one of the archipelago’s leading destinations. First came Paradisus by Meliá Fuerteventura, followed more recently by Zel Fuerteventura (the lifestyle brand created by Rafael Nadal in partnership with Meliá Hotels International). Set side by side, the two resorts form the Atlantic’s first wellness hub, set within a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Their privileged location on Sotavento beach completes the experience, with stretches of white sand and crystal-clear waters synonymous with the island.

    Fuerteventura is also recognized as one of the world's best destinations for water sports, particularly windsurfing and kitesurfing. The area surrounding both hotels is home to René Egli by Meliá, a renowned water sports center. And beyond its coastline, the island continues to stand out. Charming villages such as La Oliva are home to a newly introduced generation of boutique projects, including Casa Montelongo, one of the area's hidden gems. With the spectacular Corralejo Dunes, traditional Majorero cheese, and dramatic volcanic and desert landscapes contrasting with idyllic beaches, Fuerteventura is emerging as the ideal destination for travelers seeking a holiday centered on sport, wellness, relaxation, and reconnection. —Maria Ángeles Cano.

    Go for: a vibrant city finally getting its moment in the spotlight.

    Beyond Liepāja's beaches, converted historic and Soviet-era buildings are a reason to visit this cultural hub in 2027.

    Plenty of the most seasoned travelers have never heard of Liepāja. That’s about to change: the Baltic coastal city has been named a European Capital of Culture in 2027, bringing a year-long program of public art, performances, and festivals with an allocated $11 million in funding. Curious visitors casting their gaze towards the little-known city will discover art-nouveau architecture, an atmospheric former naval district, and one of the longest urban beaches in Northern Europe.

    It has been revealed that it’s certainly smaller and considerably less visited than Riga, but the repurposed historic and Soviet-era spaces are strangely wonderful. Wiktorija, a former cinema dating from 1913, now operates as a multi-use cultural venue hosting everything from poetry evenings to rock concerts. Take a guided tour around Karosta, the former Tsarist and Soviet naval district, to explore the history of landmarks like the striking St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral. The Great Amber Concert Hall, meanwhile, is home to the Liepāja Symphony Orchestra, the oldest in the Baltics, which is already expanding its program ahead of 2027. Rooted firmly in the present rather than the Soviet past are businesses like MO Liepāja in Julianna's Courtyard, a cluster of restored industrial buildings along the Trade Canal now housing restaurants, bars, and creative outposts such as local surfboard maker Drtyboards. —Amber Gibson.

    Go for: a charm-packed city break, with latest hotels and gorgeous coastal scenes to boot.

    Naples will host the Louis Vuitton 38th America's Cup next summer.

    As for where to rest your head? Rocco Forte Hotels will open a 46-suite stay in the 16th-century Palazzo Sirignano.

    Gritty and pretty, chaotic and cultured, ancient and contemporary, Naples is one of Italy's most exhilarating cities. In 2027, the Campanian capital will host the Louis Vuitton 38th America's Cup (July 10 to 18), an event that has accelerated the regeneration of the industrial Bagnoli waterfront. Away from the waves, the hospitality scene is evolving, too. Rocco Forte Hotels will open its first Naples property, a 46-suite retreat occupying the 16th-century Palazzo Sirignano, restored by architect Michele Bönan, and complete with a rooftop pool looking out over the Bay of Naples and Mount Vesuvius.

    Sources indicate that but Naples has never needed another reason to visit, with masterpieces such as Caravaggio's The Seven Works of Mercy and Giuseppe Sanmartino's Veiled Christ, and the antiquities of its National Archaeological Museum, whose forthcoming second site, Mann II, will bring thousands of artifacts out of storage. The city’s contemporary art scene continues to evolve at the Madre Museum, which recently welcomed internationally acclaimed curator Eugenio Viola as its newly introduced director. Nearby, Pompeii and Herculaneum agricultural parks remain as compelling as ever. And then, of course, there’s the warmth and spirit of the Neapolitan people.

    According to recent reports, da Attilio, Concettina ai Tre Santi, 50 Kalò, Diego Vitagliano, and Pizzaria La Notizia are practically compulsory for pizza, but there’s more to the city’s rich food scene. Donna Teresa and Mimì alla Ferrovia are among the beloved mainstays serving some of the finest traditional Neapolitan cuisine. —Jaclyn de Giorgio.

    Go for: an under-the-radar Ionian gem.

    Parga is the kind of Grecian destination every traveler hopes to find: easy to reach, yet seemingly under the radar. Latest hotels in 2026 and 2027 add to the appeal, without blowing its cover.

    Recent findings suggest that glittering Ionian water, pine-clad hills tumbling into a colorful harbor, and a Venetian castle above it all: Parga is undoubtedly picturesque. Yet this little corner of the Greek mainland remains surprisingly under the radar. Its old town is made for slow wandering, leisurely lunching on seafood or traditional Greek mezze at waterfront tavernas, and exploring seriously beautiful beaches such as Valtos, a gold sand bay with award-winning Blue Flag credentials. Inland, meanwhile, the Acheron River makes a heavenly setting for horseback riding, rafting, canyon walks, and swimming.

    Sources indicate that part of Parga’s appeal is how easy it is to reach: Tiny-but-mighty Preveza Airport is only an hour away, making this feel like a secret without the schlep. Parga Beach Resort, directly on Valtos Beach, makes a particularly excellent base. Its new beachfront suites, released in late summer 2026, sleep up to two adults and four children. A regular water taxi nips around the bay to Parga town, turning supper in that spectacular harbor into part of the adventure. The 2027 opening of Varko Bay nearby will add another high-end stay, with villas, a spa, sandy beaches, and a private marina. —Zoe Cook.

    #180033. 16 Incredible Hotels in Morocco Whether You’re Looking for a Royal Riad or a Kitesurfing Sanctuary

    📅 10 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2882 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    16 Incredible Hotels in Morocco Whether You’re Looking for a Royal Riad or a Kitesurfing Sanctuary

    📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task.
    • Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030.
    • In a recent development, perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task. Whether you’re looking for a charming riad stay in Marrakech, yearn for serenity and seclusion in the Atlas Mountains or proposal to immerse yourself in the Agafay desert, there’s so more to this colorful country than the promise of winter sun. It’s perhaps obvious, then, why Morocco has long since been favored by the fashionable jet set crowd, and has become home to so many notable hotel addresses. Some are so lavish they veer on palaces, others are romantically reimagined farmhouses or bohemian beachside boltholes.

    Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030. One of the biggest changes is the multi-million dollar rail expansion project, which will connect Kenitra with Marrakech, via Rabat and Casablanca. On the hotel front, Four Seasons is set to open a new address in Tangier, while Virgin Limited Edition intends to open a hotel near Marrakech. For the latest and greatest addresses, here is our pick of the best hotels in Morocco.

    The pool at El Fenn in Marrakech.

    In a recent development, perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world. Jnane Rumi—the Garden of Rumi—sits squarely within this tradition in the Palmeraie, Marrakech’s historic palm grove. It was designed by Tunisian-born Charles Boccara as a private home and has just 12 rooms: 7 in the mansion, 4 garden pavilions, and 1 private villa. Boccara grew up in Casablanca and graduated from the Beaux-Arts de Paris, and this mini manor house—with its arches and domes, expressive use of local materials, and elegantly ­mullioned windows that connect the house with a glorious garden of centenarian palms and pistachio trees—embodies his elegant Euro-Maghrebi style. It’s a seductive oasis that ­naturally gathers life, which is why owners Gert-Jan van den Bergh, an art-restitution lawyer, and his somatic-therapist wife, Corinne, felt compelled to transform it into a ­cultural hub, platforming contemporary Moroccan artists and designers, and curating art events and creative retreats. —Paula Hardy.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Check Availability at Priceline.

    It has been revealed that set between the mountains and the sea, this smart family-friendly resort and discreet spa retreat was conceived and built by King Mohammed VI as a showcase for the artisanal skills and flair that are a cornerstone of Morocco’s cultural heritage. The Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay houses more than 2,000 works of art in an astounding showcase for Moroccan craftsmanship and artisanal skills. Set on a 700-meter private beachfront along the so-called Moroccan Riviera, it sits low within a landscaped garden scented with rosemary, sage lavender, and mint. While there are some big name resorts further along the coastline including Sofitel and Ritz Carlton, this the first home-grown luxury offering and stands head and shoulders above the others for its service (all staff are trained at Royal Mansour’s own hospitality school) and obsessive attention to detail, as well as its sustainable practices. It’s also open year-round for dedicated spa-goers who come for Longevity programs of varying time frames in the largest and most professional med spa in Northern Africa. —Catherine Fairweather.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Industry observers note that A shiny, super-sized proposition from Four Seasons, successfully incorporating beautiful Moroccan touches in the shared areas and sleek luxury in the private spaces. This would be an ideal three- or four-night stop for a spot of sightseeing and a lot of pampering as part of a wider Moroccan tour, with the city itself being a serene introduction to what is a very colorful and frenetic country. The true headliner here is the newly opened spa, which has a thorough menu and high-end treatments for every mood, with the opportunity to relax by the magnificent indoor pool afterwards. There’s an effortless blending of old and newly introduced, and a devotion to looking after the guest. Palatial, imposing, luxurious, with an impressive attention to detail, Four Seasons’ newest Moroccan property makes you feel like a modern day sultan. —Matt Charlton.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that three years after opening La Sultana Marrakech in 2004, the owners sought a quieter, more intimate spot to unveil their second Moroccan hotel. The result was La Sultana’s beachy sanctuary of restorative wellness, slotted between acres of flourishing farmland and a tranquil lagoon sheltered from the roaring Atlantic. Sustainable, sea-to-table dining is central to the La Sultana experience, and seafood lovers will be glad to hear that oysters are the star dish, with five oyster beds scattered across the lagoon. All rooms have their own elegant personality, and with just 12 to choose from, the precision which has gone into each design is palpable. The Treehouse Suite is a personal favorite, centred around a real eucalyptus tree which permeates through the bedroom floor and ceiling. There’s a lovely cathedral-inspired spa exclusive to guests, with pool, hot tub, sauna, and five treatment rooms, as well as a nearly 150-foot infinity pool outside, seamlessly seeping into the sea at high tide. —Layla Quaedvlieg.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    The rocky sparseness of Morocco’s Agafay desert has long attracted travelers wanting a break from the sensory explosions of Marrakech. It’s an ideal landing spot for the Habitas group, which since 2016 has been setting up its minimalist, sustainable eco-retreats in places like Mexico, Namibia, and Saudi Arabia. Their oasis among the lunar dunes eschews bells and whistles in favor of communal vibes and engagement with nature—or “luxury for the soul,” as the founders call it. They've now applied their ethos to Agafay’s 41 Berber-inspired tents and lodges. Each en suite tent—solar-powered, with eco-bathrooms—embodies stylish pared-down-ness: no minibars or TVs, just wooden floors and earthy cream and ochre tones reminiscent of the regional rock.

    Sources indicate that weekenders escaping European cities sink into poufs and Berber rugs inside the communal glass-wrapped lounge. On the semi-open dining veranda, beneath raffia lamps, they tuck into lamb slow-cooked in the underground oven before knocking back market sangrias by the open-air bar, silhouetted against the Atlas Mountains and flame-red sunsets that give way to heavenly constellations. This is what travel is about—less guilt and more meaning amid tranquillity, good conversation, and cleansing nature. —Noo Saro-Wiwa.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Recent findings suggest that with a name as reputable as Nobu on the door, good service, and an even better restaurant offering are practically scribed into the brickwork. Marrakech is the brand's first foray into Africa, and its interiors remain respectful of the location, capturing a different kind of aesthetic that sets it apart from its Mediterranean cousins. The location is one to celebrate. From here, you can walk to the medina and the souks, or arrange drivers to take you further afield via the concierge, who suggests tours to the Atlas mountains, desert picnics, and cultural experiences like camel rides. The rooftop is as beautiful as the 360-degree views it offers, and watching the sun cast ombre shades of pink and orange across the sky before it sinks behind the horizon is best accompanied by a signature cocktail or a serving of mint tea—poured from an elaborate silver-tone pot, of course. Every bedroom is a suite bedecked in mahogany wood and rich furnishings. —Sarah Leigh Bannerman.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    At the Royal Mansour Marrakech, located inside the medina, the draw is privacy—its beautifully tiled riads have their own pools dotting lush gardens that are made for afternoon strolls. The palatial resort, founded by King Mohammed VI to showcase the best of Moroccan artistry and hospitality, was built over three years by 1,200 master craftsmen. It’s a swoon-worthy showpiece of Moroccan decorative art.

    Recent findings suggest that each of the 53 individual three-story riads comprises a mini courtyard (with a canopy that automatically unfurls if rain is detected); a sumptuously appointed living room; an equally dazzling bedroom with silk-covered walls, hand-painted arched doorways, and generous MarocMaroc bath amenities; and a private rooftop terrace with a fireplace. Guests are tended to by a gracious staff, in particular a butler who appears silently through the riad’s kitchen service entry.

    Industry observers note that although Djemaa el Fna square is within walking distance, there’s much to keep you ensconced in this city sanctuary, including indoor and outdoor pools, a magnificent spa, and two superb restaurants, La Grande Table Marocaine and La Grande Table Française , as well as the indoor-outdoor La Table, which serves a formally presented breakfast and lunch by white-gloved staff. —Todd Plummer.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    This is where Charlie Chaplin and Churchill chose to hole up, and Hitchcock filmed The Man Who Knew Too Much. Reinvigorated by designer Jacques Garcia, it had a spectacular reopening in 2009. Retreat from the hubbub to the huge gardens, with their beekeepers, lemon trees, secret ice-cream parlor, and the loveliest pool with a palm tree in the middle. The Sunday poolside brunch—tagines, grilled fish, pizza flatbreads—is excellent for hungry children, as is eating in Le Marocain to the sounds of a traditional oud (a bit like a lute). For a riad-style stay, there are three houses on the grounds, but the rooms with views out to the Koutoubia Mosque and over the rooftops of the Red City are the ones that give you the best sense of place. Pick up neon earthenware jugs, Berber-style rugs, and baskets at Upcoming York designer Martin Raffone’s MaisonLAB in Guéliz.

    Check Availability at Hotels.com.

    All kasbahs are a kind of oasis of calm behind fortified walls, and Kasbah Tamadot is one of the very finest in Morocco. Its name means “soft breeze” in the local Berber language, evoking the reprieve it offers in the shadow of the Atlas Mountains. First built over a century ago as a home for a local governor, it became part of the Virgin Limited Edition Collection in 2005. Now reopened following substantial damage from the 2023 earthquake, Tamadot is a lavish yet quirky Amazigh castle with exquisite carved doors and intimate courtyards, secret passageways, and terraces of reflecting pools strewn with rose petals.

    It's furnished with the extraordinary collections of the previous owner, a Venetian antiquarian named Luciano Tempo, which were included when Richard Branson purchased the place. Huge bronze and wooden chests that might have carried Barbarossa’s loot stand in corners. In rambling gardens, pathways meander beneath trellises of jasmine while apple trees frame the cabanas around the swimming pool. In addition to atmospheric rooms in the old kasbah, accommodations offer a step-up in luxury with 10 glamorous Berber tents in the gardens and six luxurious riads (lovely three-bedroom suites with private pools). —Stanley Stewart.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Integrating opulence in just the right measure is a difficult task, but this five-star hotel (once home to the king's advisor) pulls it off perfectly. After you enter the building with its cream-colored walls, you’ll find yourself in the lobby, a luminous space with nearly 40-foot ceilings. It’s the first hint that this hotel does everything in style: from the eight acres of landscaped grounds to the dramatic lamps that illuminate the corridor leading to the Crudo restaurant and the photogenic swimming pool, where you’ll lose track of time under the Mediterranean sun.

    The hotel’s 133 rooms are an amalgam of elements that celebrate the country’s craft traditions with fretwork wooden screens, mosaics, and bespoke fabrics created by local artisans. The Fairmont Tazi Palace’s massive wellness center includes 10 treatment rooms, a private spa, a solarium, a hammam you won’t want to leave, and sunny Andalusian-style gardens that lead to a secluded vitality pool. Let yourself unwind before refueling at one of the four restaurants, where ingredients are pulled from the hotel’s own orchard and kitchen garden. —Lidia González.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    According to recent reports, it’s easy to forget what a game-changer El Fenn was when it opened two decades ago on the edge of the medina with just six jewel-toned bedrooms and a rooftop that felt like a fabulous house party. It stitched itself into the fabric of the Red City and redefined its aesthetic with color-clashing walls and lounges of thickly woven Berber and velvet fabrics, Moorish keyhole archways, and orange trees.

    Like the best hotels, it has moved—and expanded—with the times. Co-owner Vanessa Branson has gradually bought up the crumbling neighboring riads to create a wondrous labyrinth of 13 interconnected buildings, 3 pools, and 41 bedrooms in blush pinks, mustards, and acid yellows. Some have zellige tiles, others hand-stitched camel leather floors and carved wooden ceilings, all offset with pop art and bright contemporary installations.

    In a recent development, I recently stayed in one of the “cozy” rooms, behind an ornate cedar door. Between the hand-plastered traditional tadelakt wall, contemporary dot painting, and mother-of-pearl chandelier, it’s nearly impossible to tell old from latest, a result of using local artisans, natural fabrics, and upcycled furniture. Amid the rooftop’s pool, sunbeds and pops of color, the old magic of Marrakech endures. —Chloe Sachdev.

    Industry observers note that connecting with nature in Morocco's beauty spot, where you can be as active or as laid-back as you like, all while enjoying the breathtaking backdrop of the Atlas Mountains. Just 20 minutes outside the heart of Marrakech, the landscape starts to change—countless olive groves, tall leafy palms, and fragrant argan and lemon trees. The distant views of the Atlas Mountains paint the scene, but it's the grand arch at the resort’s entrance that sets the tone of sheer majesty. Step through the iconic Fairmont swinging doors and you’re greeted by towering ceilings, marble accents, plush furnishings, and an endless sense of chic glamour.

    The main bar, Le Bar, dressed in a sleek black-and-gold scheme, feels like a scene straight out of a James Bond film. Jaw-dropping Moroccan chandeliers add to the extravagant spirit and five-star quality. Outside, 570 acres of lush green landscape await, showcasing Marrakech’s horticultural prowess. Home to an 18-hole golf course and a pampering spa, it’s the ultimate base for wellness seekers, romantic couples, families, and culture vultures keen to experience the crème de la crème of Marrakech’s idyllic rural scene.

    It has been revealed that this rare palm-framed fantasyland near Ouarzazate, whose name translates from Arabic as “House of Dreams,” was conjured20 years ago, from the wild imagination of a Parisian creative. Thierry Teyssier re-envisaged the 200-year-old ochre kasbah and its rammed-earth ramparts to honor its Berber heritage with authenticity, elegance, and an unrivaled romance. Spells at the hideaway are more magical than ever, with the handful of rooms in the North African castle joined by spacious suites at the edge of the Louis Benech–landscaped grounds.

    According to recent reports, teyssier’s past lives as a theater actor and event planner keep him challenging traditional hospitality as a disrupter and storyteller: Every soul-stirring scene is art-directed and choreographed to enchant, with delicate, tactile interiors, seductive scents, and unexpected curios at every turn. Surrendering to Dar Ahlam’s rare rhythm is akin to participating in immersive theatre, with unprompted poolside pomegranate juices, candlelit Berber tents for secret suppers, and personally addressed hand-penned scrolls or other gifts at bedtime. Guests can explore vast desert-scapes by four-by-four, or let the staff plan a picnic in a villager’s vegetable garden. There is no lobby, restaurant, or bar, just beautiful spaces unfettered by telephones, menus, or minibars. —Juliet Kinsman.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Royal Mansour, owned by Morocco’s royal family, can be credited as one of Marrakech’s (if not Morocco’s) finest stays: a romantic riad, where luxury is distinctly of the old-world variety. Naturally, the announcement of a second location sent the travel industry into a titter. Heads up, though: Anyone expecting a mirror image of Royal Mansour Marrakech is going to be surprised. While the level of service and luxury at the new location (in the once-home of the 1953-built El Mansour hotel) follows the first property’s lead, the experience, and especially the aesthetic, is a departure. There are 149 rooms, with three categories of suites, and several “apartment” offerings.

    Sources indicate that there are four restaurants: The brasserie serves delicious French classics, and at the sushi bar, chefs from Japan take on the task of bringing omakase to a Moroccan audience. For Moroccan food, head up to the 23rd floor. Just before sunset, the room of mirrors and gold comes alive in the light. Stick around for delicious sweet baghrir bread, fried spinach cheese briouat, and naturally, more tajines. The views over the city aren’t bad either. —Megan Spurrell.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    How we choose the best hotels in Morocco.

    Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

    #180032. Industry News: Which AI Bots Can Help You Book Travel?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1993 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Which AI Bots Can Help You Book Travel?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A multitude of upcoming start ups promise AI assistants will “handle your travel.” I’m skeptical of anything that promises to handle my travel, mostly because I’ve spent years learning exactly where airline websites like to hide the landmines and sharing it with our audience.
    • Industry observers note that to be clear, this is not a test of chatbots that spit out a list of flights and then send you off to do the work yourself.
    • According to recent reports, I gave the a Grok Bot (a single AI agent) the same basic trip on every airline: Pittsburgh (PIT) to Fort Myers (RSW), one way, on Tuesday, December 15, 2026, for four adults.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, A multitude of upcoming start ups promise AI assistants will “handle your travel.” I’m skeptical of anything that promises to handle my travel, mostly because I’ve spent years learning exactly where airline websites like to hide the landmines and sharing it with our audience. But following Kirby’s (United’s) statement that AI bots would be blocked from its sites, I got curious about where we are with airlines and bots. I wanted to see what happens when an AI agent, one that drives a real web browser the way you or I would (in this case, Grok as ChatGPT, and Claude work differently), sits down at the airline’s own website and tries to book a real itinerary.

    Industry observers note that to be clear, this is not a test of chatbots that spit out a list of flights and then send you off to do the work yourself. The question here is narrower and more practical. Can an agentic AI search, pick a fare, fill in the forms and get a family of four to the payment page without a human bailing it out? And just as interesting, which airlines let it in the door at all? For this hypothesis, I presumed United would be a certain “no” but what about the others?

    According to recent reports, I gave the a Grok Bot (a single AI agent) the same basic trip on every airline: Pittsburgh (PIT) to Fort Myers (RSW), one way, on Tuesday, December 15, 2026, for four adults. On American, I used a real award rebooking for my own family while signed in to my AAdvantage account. On Delta, United and Southwest, the agent shopped cash fares while signed out. Grok is unique in two ways, first that it has its “own computer” where it runs your searches instead of yours, and second, that it can securely store your login credentials and operate as you would but it never sees those credentials (don’t ask me how.) I understand that Muse may have some of the same features, but my setup experience there was not as straight forward and I don’t need a fifth AI tool even if it’s integrated into my existing Instagram and Facebook accounts.

    It has been revealed that I drew one firm line. The agent could go as far as the passenger or payment page, but nothing got purchased in any of these tests. Card details, CVVs and the final “Purchase” click stayed with me and I never processed any of them.

    American was the most realistic test and also the most frustrating. The agent had no trouble with the award search on aa.com using my account logged in. It pulled up 40 results for PIT to RSW, with Main Cabin at 10,500 miles one way per person and First at 25,500 miles.

    Recent findings suggest that it found AA 3030 acceptable flights from Pittsburgh to Charlotte, connecting to Fort Myers, in Main Cabin for 42,000 miles plus $22.40 for all four of us. If I wanted to, I could train the AI to understand whether I would want a morning or evening flight typically, an acceptable layover range, it could look at my schedule and ensure that we have sufficient time to get to a meeting and work around my schedule and preferences, not just my price. This test didn’t need all of that.

    It got that itinerary all the way to “Review and pay.” Then the friction started. My saved card on the account required the CVV to be entered again, which the agent could not supply (and, frankly, should not have). While that was being sorted out, the checkout session expired.

    In a recent development, when the agent rebuilt the cart, aa.com threw up its “Please confirm you’re a human” challenge with an “I’m not a robot” box. The AI dutifully lied but identified where and how that was running. That page comes from a bot manager, which assigns every visitor a score from human to bot and can raise that score as the same visitor keeps making requests. Rebuilding a cart several times looks automated (because it was.) At that point a human had to step in.

    In a recent development, I’d rate this as a 90% solution with a final human check and ultimate purchase as the last 10% to complete. This is likely a best case scenario to keep control of your miles or money and ensure what you book is correct.

    Delta was the cleanest run of the bunch. The agent set up the one-way search, added four passengers, picked the date and landed on a results page with flights connecting in Atlanta and arriving after 9pm, at $192 per person in Main because this one was not a logged in redemption.

    From there it handled the Basic vs Main Classic choice, clicked past the upsell screens (an airline’s worst nightmare) and reached “Review and Pay” with a trip total of just under $965 for four in Main Classic. No captcha, no “are you human”, nothing. If Delta’s site was suspicious of my agent, it did not show it. There was no resistance. I flag this as an advantage for Delta, because tech forward clients will love that they can get an entire booking done start to finish without their intervention.

    Industry observers note that united, like Delta, also let the agent through to the end of my test, but it took more attempts. The date field was finicky, with the calendar jumping ahead to January and February 2027 before the agent got back to December as I watched it work. The travelers dialog took several retries before it stopped saying “1 Adult” and accepted four. Not as smooth as Delta, but not a total block which I would have thought they’d install.

    Industry observers note that once the search ran, the agent took the first result (which it did not do for the others) a 6 AM departure via Washington Dulles, and correctly skipped Basic Economy (United makes you tick a “Basic Economy works for me” box first) in favor of the Standard fare. That is a reasonable choice for a family, but my kids would have something to say about a 6 AM departure, which is a good reminder that an AI agent only knows the preferences you give it.

    It has been revealed that it then reached the “Traveler Info” page with a total of $964.80, which is, amusingly (but from a competitive standpoint, unsurprising), the exact same total Delta revealed for four people. No captcha appeared on United at any point.

    Southwest ended up with the best itinerary and the lowest price. The first result was a nonstop leaving Pittsburgh at 9:50 AM and arriving in Fort Myers at 12:30 PM. The agent chose the Choice fare at $222 per person, for a total of $885.60 for four. If it only it knew my kids, this nonstop would be the clear winner even if the price wasn’t better than United and Delta. That noted, I would also need to input information about what’s preferred when comparing miles and points, and my personal valuation so that it doesn’t choose even an $885 one-way for four people if American happened to be running 5,000-mile one-ways.

    Still, it got to the “Passengers” page, step 2 of 5, without any bot restrictions.

    This isn’t an entirely comprehensively list as not all of them were useful for both the Live And Let’s Fly audience as well as my purposes. But what I did do is ask the AI to check whether each airline has its own AI assistants that can actually search, book, change or cancel a flight, or whether those tools just answer FAQs and hand you to a person.

    According to recent reports, alaska is the one that has built something close to a trip-planning AI. Its “Trip inspiration with AI” tool, Alaska Inspires, sits in the Book menu on alaskaair.com. Alaska and Microsoft (I suspect an even further neutered version of Co-Pilot) say you can type or speak a request in plain language, get destination ideas, and discover, compare and book in the same flow. In a March 2025 interview, Alaska’s director of innovation, Bernadette Berger, gave examples like “Where can I go in Europe for under 80k miles?” Microsoft’s write-up claims a 7% conversion rate versus 5% for the standard booking widget. My AI was not able to run my booking through Inspires so this would be a failure in my experience but I am willing to try again using different parameters.

    JetBlue does have a customer-service AI but I was unsuccessful in attempting to advance it further.

    Breeze Airways has gone further on digital customer care than most low-cost carriers. VP of Guest Experience Danny Cox, says Breeze uses Gladly’s generative “Answer Threads” tool to present change and cancellation options in chat or SMS, and that AI fully resolves 37% of conversations. That is post-booking help, not a bot that will shop a upcoming itinerary for you. Breeze’s own contact pages blocked my lookup, so I could not independently confirm how the current chat or text flow works for a brand-new booking. That would be a failure but again, I suspect a logged in account might perform better.

    Sources indicate that allegiant does put a bot on its site but this is for customer service alone. Sun Country and JSX are even thinner on the consumer-facing side and my bot failed for all of these carriers too.

    Recent findings suggest that on the cash side, AI agents can already do the boring part of booking. All three cash bookings reached a passenger or payment page, and none of them hit a captcha. The agent picked sensible fares, navigated upsell screens and dealt with clunky widgets on its own, even if United’s date picker and Southwest’s sluggish buttons cost it some time. Adding that personal context could make this a very practical option.

    Industry observers note that the real wall is at the end. Payment details, CVVs and timed checkout sessions are designed to need a human, and I think that is fine. The bigger issue is bot detection because it wasn’t really built to detect or negate AI bots but general hacks that could operate massive attacks on the sites. American is the airline that blocked my agent outright, and it happened on the most complex booking of the test, involving award miles and a signed-in account. Whether that was because of the account, the repeated cart rebuilds or just AA’s settings that day, the result was the same.

    But United is the only one that has said it won’t allow AI bots and absolutely did.

    Out of all of the tests, Delta was the easiest and had me most encouraged, while United and Southwest made it harder but not impossible and not specifically against AI, just the design of the site. American was the only one that really made it difficult and that shocked me. This test, and travelers using these tools for booking purposes are narrow at the moment but as AI agents/bots continue to advance and become normalized, the carriers will likely do something more robust. That stated, there could be a strong advantage for those that are “AI-friendly.” Competitive markets like Los Angeles and New York might see more flights sold on Delta from indifferent travelers solely because it’s easier. The real question becomes how comfortable the general public becomes and with that, hopefully not too comfortable or websites will crash from users searching flights hundreds of times a day.

    According to recent reports, what do you think? Would you store your logins? Would you entrust an AI bot or agent to return travel results for you even if you have to complete the purchase on your own?

    Report: Lufthansa to Cut 1,000 Jobs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (230 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lufthansa Group aims to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.
    • According to recent reports, the airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal.
    • Firm leaders mentioned their 2024 turnaround strategy, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa Group aims to lay off around 1,000 full-time workers at its flagship carrier as elevated fuel prices and service disruptions continue to undercut earnings.

    According to recent reports, the airline group disclosed the cuts in a letter sent to employees and seen by Dow Jones Newswire, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reductions will target Lufthansa’s hubs in Frankfurt and Munich.

    Firm leaders mentioned their 2024 turnaround strategy, initially expected to boost earnings by €2.5 billion over four years, is no longer enough to keep the brand on solid financial ground.

    “The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action, and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation,” the letter mentioned.

    Lufthansa failed to reach an agreement with its pilot union earlier this week, setting the stage for a possible work stoppage. The impasse has already resulted in two short strikes, one in February, the other in March.

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa Group has spoken openly about the damage caused by higher fuel prices over the last nine months. Over the summer, it retired aircraft, cut routes, and warned that layoffs were likely unless prices eased.

    According to EuroNews, Lufthansa has lost on average about €20 million per month since the start of the year.

    Latest Update: The 10 Best Places to Retire in the US

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
