    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the problem is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Fresh York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the problem.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they initiative to bring up a vote next year.

    In a recent development, senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump noted, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Recent findings suggest that trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    Recent findings suggest that “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    An Alaska Airlines Boeing 737-800 has been temporarily grounded in Upcoming York after colliding with a catering vehicle ahead of a flight to San Francisco International (SFO). Such was the extent of the damage that the flight ended up having to be canceled. A similar incident also befell a United Airlines Airbus A320 this year, which resulted in the jet being taken out of service for good. Let's examine Monday's events.

    According to recent reports, alaska Airlines flight AS41 is a daily scheduled service from New York to San Francisco. It is one of the carrier's longest transcontinental flights, with a block time of six hours and 41 minutes between its planned departure from JFK at 5:25 PM and its scheduled arrival into the Bay Area at 9:06 PM (all times local). The iteration of this flight on Monday, November 23, however, ended up having to be canceled.

    This, as seen in the clip above, was due to the jet having been hit by a catering truck on the ground at JFK ahead of its departure. The Aviation Safety Network reported that "the ventral strake of the left-hand split scimitar winglet" bore the brunt of the damage, which was severe enough to take the jet out of service. Passengers were then told that the damaged Boeing 737 would return to the gate to deplane.

    Simple Flying has reached out to Alaska Airlines for further information on this incident. We will patch our coverage upon receiving a statement from the carrier.

    Sources indicate that winglets play an important role in reducing drag and improving fuel efficiency, but they are also exposed to potential damage during ground operations, particularly when aircraft are moving around busy airport aprons. Even minimal damage can require inspections and repairs before an aircraft is cleared to fly again. Although the damage was enough to cancel the flight, the aircraft's eventual return to service will depend on the extent of the damage and the repairs required.

    For the passengers impacted by Monday evening's cancelation of flight AS41, Alaska Airlines appears to have scheduled an extra flight to San Francisco on Tuesday morning, numbered AS9230, which is scheduled to depart JFK at 9:00 AM. The carrier schedules up to four flights a day between New York JFK and San Francisco, with departures spread throughout the day to optimize connectivity.

    Recent findings suggest that according to fleet data from ch-aviation, N548AS is one of 59 examples of the Boeing 737-800 that Alaska Airlines presently has at its disposal. These narrowbody twinjets are 18.7 years old on average, although N548AS is one of the more senior examples, having first flown 21.45 years ago. It was delivered to Alaska Airlines on July 1, 2005, and it currently seats 161 passengers across two classes.

    Sources indicate that it remains to be seen exactly how badly N548AS has been damaged as a result of its ground collision on Monday evening. However, such incidents can end up being more terminal for older aircraft, such as N470UA, a United Airlines Airbus A320-200 that was hit by a truck in Washington in May 2026.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday demonstrated how poisonous the politics could become.

    Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” stated Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking notable.”.

    Sources indicate that johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    Industry observers note that "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he mentioned on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson mentioned Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    It has been revealed that johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

    Sources indicate that there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle noted they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    • Recent findings suggest that russell has a museum of his own in Great Falls, Mont., but he’s also got a suite of revelatory galleries at the Montana Heritage Center in Helena, my starting point as I explored the state from west to east.
    • Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    Today I’ll write about Big Sky Country — Montana. I’d never been. The Mountain States aren’t the place to go for Raphaels, Rembrandts, and Renoirs, but there are treasures to be found. What ought to be there? I very easily found my answer: Montana’s own Charles M. Russell, the perceptive, precise artist famous for his cowboy pictures but proudest of his scenes of Montana’s Chippewa, Blood Indian, and Lakota Natives. At 16, Russell (1864–1926) left school in Missouri to work on a sheep ranch in Montana. He lived under those spacious skies for the rest of his life, making thousands of works of art. A contemporary of Frederic Remington, he’s less known but just as good if not better.

    Recent findings suggest that russell has a museum of his own in Great Falls, Mont., but he’s also got a suite of revelatory galleries at the Montana Heritage Center in Helena, my starting point as I explored the state from west to east. The Heritage Center, whose galleries are filled with art and artifacts from Montana’s Historical Society, opened late last year after a $160 million expansion and renovation. It’s wonderful. The Russell section is more or less chronological and a mix of art, hagiography, and atmosphere. I loved it. The entire new complex is great. It’s got a Russell section as well as multiple galleries on Montana’s history.

    Sources indicate that brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    5 Air Force Bases Spending Hundreds Of Millions To Rebuild Cold War-Era Runways

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that today, modern military aviation is a blend of innovations so advanced that most people are prohibited from knowing all the details, and Cold War-era technology.
    • It has been revealed that discussions about this difference usually center on aircraft, but another area where this is prominent is with airfields.
    • According to recent reports, while most bases were subsequently upgraded, they have to accommodate planes like the F-35 Lightning II and the B-21 Raider today, and the infrastructure itself is aging.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that today, modern military aviation is a blend of innovations so advanced that most people are prohibited from knowing all the details, and Cold War-era technology. Although planes like the B-52 are ancient, the math works out because they're effective in the roles that they serve, while upcoming planes are developed for more demanding missions where technological improvements make a significant difference.

    It has been revealed that discussions about this difference usually center on aircraft, but another area where this is prominent is with airfields. Many United States Air Force (USAF) bases were constructed during the Second World War and the Cold War, initially designed for propeller-driven aircraft and early jets.

    According to recent reports, while most bases were subsequently upgraded, they have to accommodate planes like the F-35 Lightning II and the B-21 Raider today, and the infrastructure itself is aging. As such, the USAF is investing in upgrading these bases, with runways as the key focus.

    Selfridge Air National Guard Base at the moment operates with one runway, 01/19, which is 9,000 feet (2,743 meters) long. With the base set to start receiving upcoming aircraft in 2028, the state of Michigan is funding an airfield expansion that will relocate and extend the runway and add two new taxiways connecting to it.

    According to recent reports, the project is estimated to cost Michigan $152 million, and the bill's passage also includes nearly $1 billion in federal funding and grants to modernize the base as a whole. Selfridge right now hosts the Fairchild Republic A-10 Thunderbolt II and the Boeing KC-135R Stratotanker, but the Air National Guard intends to begin stationing the Boeing F-15EX Strike Eagle II and KC-46 Pegasus starting in 2028. These aircraft are larger and heavier than their predecessors, requiring a latest movement area design, and the shift also moves the airport's primary flight path away from nearby residential neighborhoods. This will therefore decrease the noise impact of aircraft operating in the vicinity.

    Industry observers note that the project will require the nearby Rosso Highway and local utility lines to be relocated, and there has been controversy over how it is being funded. In addition, there have been disputes with local landowners over the compensation figures for the acquired land, as well as with environmental activists, because the project will impact between six and nine acres of wetlands in the area.

    It has been revealed that ellsworth Air Force Base is home to the 28th Bomb Wing, one of only two USAF wings that operate the Rockwell B-1B Lancer. In addition, the 89th Attack Squadron, which operates the General Atomics MQ-9A Reaper drone and is part of the 432nd Wing, is also based out of Ellsworth.

    Sources indicate that in 2019, Ellsworth was selected as the preferred base to host the first formal training unit and operational bombing unit for the upcoming Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider, which will become the USAF's primary bomber. To prepare for the aircraft, Ellsworth spent $129.5 million to upgrade its 13,497-foot (4,113-meter) runway. This involved replacing the top 12 inches (30.48 centimeters) of the runway center keel while also rebuilding both runway overruns.

    In addition, one taxiway was fully refurbished, while another was partially refurbished. The lighting system was upgraded for a 50-year lifespan, and the entire runway was fully rebuilt using 106,000 tons of concrete cement, 105 miles of joint sealing, and 83 miles of electrical conduit. The runway reconstruction was initially planned to take place over three years.

    It has been revealed that however, due to operational needs, the project was compressed and completed in December 2025, just ten months after construction began. The project displaced 17 B-1B Lancers and roughly 800 service personnel to nearby Grand Forks Air Force Base, but the rapid completion time reduced the impact of the disruption. It's right now anticipated that the first operational B-21 will arrive at Ellsworth in 2027, and Northrop Grumman is expanding B-21 production capacity by 25% under a February 2026 agreement.

    Tyndall Air Force Base was heavily damaged by Hurricane Michael in 2018. 484 buildings were damaged, and the storm produced 792,450 cubic yards (605,871 cubic meters) of debris. Afterward, Tyndall Air Force Base opted to fully rebuild, calling it the 'Installation of the Future.' It spent $5 billion on newly introduced facilities that would be more hurricane-resilient. The base also features new technological innovations such as gunshot detection, a real-time 3D model of Tyndall, and a possible microgrid capable of powering Tyndall independently should the main power grid go down.

    Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II Variants.

    F-35A (conventional takeoff & landing).

    F-35B (short takeoff & landing).

    As part of the project, Tyndall is refurbishing its two runways. Not only is this centered on generally refurbishing the airfield's infrastructure, but Tyndall is also looking to better meet the needs of the Lockheed F-35 Lightning II. The base received its first F-35 Lightning II in August 2023, marking a major milestone, and the USAF has planned to base three full F-35 squadrons at Tyndall. In total, Tyndall is planned to be home to over 70 operational F-35s.

    Recent findings suggest that tyndall Air Force Base is hosted by the 325th Fighter Wing, which includes the previously mentioned three F-35 squadrons. In addition, the 325th Fighter Wing also previously stationed a Lockheed F-22 Raptor training squadron at Tyndall, but the F-22s were later transferred out to make way for the F-35s. Each of the three squadrons is slated to operate 24 F-35s each, along with additional backup units. All examples are the F-35A variant, which is specifically designed for the United States Air Force.

    According to recent reports, grand Forks Air Force Base does not currently have any squadrons with manned aircraft. Instead, Grand Forks is hosted by the 319th Reconnaissance Wing, whose 348th Reconnaissance Squadron operates the Northrop Grumman RQ-4B Global Hawk Block 40 unmanned aerial vehicle.

    It has been revealed that the RQ-4B has been flying from Grand Forks since 2011, and the USAF has not stationed manned aircraft since 2010, when the USAF deactivated the base's refueling unit which operated the Boeing KC-135. In May 2026, work began on a resurfacing program for the 12,351-foot (3,764-meter) Runway 17/35.

    319th Reconnaissance Wing Primary Squadrons.

    Naval Air Station Sigonella, Italy.

    Grand Forks Air Force Base, North Dakota.

    The primary reason for the project is to address cracking and weathering in the runway, and approximately 10,270 feet (3,130 meters) of the runway will need to be repaired. This involves using a milling and overlaying process, and the entire project is expected to cost $20.4 million. It's at the moment projected that the runway milling and overlaying will take roughly six months to complete. In the meantime, the drones have been temporarily relocated to Robins Air Force Base in Georgia.

    Industry observers note that after being shifted in April, the Global Hawks were cleared to return when the runway reopened in late October. The relocation has enabled continuity of operations for the 319th Reconnaissance Wing, which also consists of geographically separated units in Italy and Japan. Notably, the flexibility of the RQ-4B platform has made the temporary relocation less disruptive than you'd otherwise expect.

    North Field is an airfield in Tinian, Mariana Islands, and is mainly known today as a tourist attraction. The airfield hasn't been used since 1946, when the United States Army Air Forces left after having no purpose for it post-World War II, and North Field is now easily accessible to the general public.

    People can drive on parts of the taxiways and runways, while the surviving administrative buildings and the airfield were designated a National Historic Landmark District for North Field's role in World War II. However, as the US continues to view China as an adversary and is preparing for potential conflict in Asia, it has turned back to North Field.

    It has been revealed that it committed around $500 million in 2024 to clearing vegetation overgrowth at the airfield and repaving North Field's movement areas. Details are limited, but it's expected that two of North Field's 7,874-foot (2,400-meter) runways will be fully refurbished by 2027, and initial flight operations at North Field already commenced in late May 2026, hosting a detachment of personnel supporting joint-force training. Despite its age, North Field is more indicative of the future than almost any other USAF airfield.

    In a recent development, increasingly, the US is positioning itself to be better prepared for a possible conflict with China, and North Field will be crucial in maintaining its desired operational level in the Indo-Pacific region. In addition, the USAF is also expanding its operations in Palau, while the upcoming B-21 Raider was designed specifically for the Indo-Pacific theater, contrasting with its Cold War-era predecessor, the B-2 Spirit.

    Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    According to recent reports, trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    Sources indicate that “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    Sources indicate that his interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    It has been revealed that “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump stated as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Latest York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    In a recent development, “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump stated, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    Sources indicate that other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of complications, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer remarked.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    Sources indicate that nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He noted it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers noted they doubted very much would come from it.

    Sources indicate that “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    According to recent reports, “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to promptly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    Industry observers note that “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    Industry observers note that john M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Ryanair Cancels All Flights To 5 Destinations: See Full List Now

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ryanair plays a critical role in Europe.
    • Due to only having 189-seat Boeing 737-800s and 197-seat 737 MAX 8-200s, Ryanair has 17% of Europe's short-haul seats for sale.
    • It'd be easy to conclude that the following places have simply stopped being served because October is when Northern Hemisphere airlines switch from summer to winter schedules based on IATA slot seasons.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ryanair plays a critical role in Europe. In November 2026, OAG data shows that the ultra-low-cost carrier has 14% of the continent's short-haul flights. In other words, the carrier provides one in every seven services.

    Due to only having 189-seat Boeing 737-800s and 197-seat 737 MAX 8-200s, Ryanair has 17% of Europe's short-haul seats for sale. More than one in every six seats is provided by the budget operator. This dominance does not mean it is immune to routes and airports being cut. Far from it, with five airports removed in October alone.

    It'd be easy to conclude that the following places have simply stopped being served because October is when Northern Hemisphere airlines switch from summer to winter schedules based on IATA slot seasons. This occurred on Sunday, October 25, with the airports all last seeing Ryanair just before that date.

    Recent findings suggest that the cuts are not seasonal, and the markets are not coming back in 2027. They have been removed from the ULCC's network, just like others were earlier in 2026, and another will be in early 2027. Some may return in the future. Ryanair had previously ditched two of them only to return later. In Volos' case, only one route (Brussels Charleroi) existed when the carrier resumed operations.

    Served By The Airline Since...?

    All Routes (Excluding The Charter Operations Of Buzz).

    Bratislava (2018-2019, 2022-2026), Dublin (2018-2026), London Stansted (2024-2026).

    Brussels Charleroi (2011-2014, 2025-2026), Frankfurt Hahn (2010-2014), Milan Bergamo (2010-2014), Rome Ciampino (2011).

    Dublin (2019-2026), London Stansted (2024-2026).

    Gdańsk (2020), London Stansted (2019-2026), Milan Bergamo (2013-2015, 2019-2026), Milan Malpensa (2020-2022), Pisa (2019, 2022), Sofia (2019), Vienna (2020-2026).

    Berlin Schönefeld (now closed; 2016-2020), Bratislava (2016-2020), Corfu (2021-2026), Malta (2019-2026), Milan Bergamo (2016-2023), Stockholm Arlanda (2021-2026), Stockholm Skavsta (2017-2020), Weeze (2016-2019), Vienna (2021-2026).

    Notice the two Turkish vacation hotspots of Bodrum and Dalaman. By no longer serving them, Ryanair has entirely pulled out of Turkey. Unsurprisingly, this was enveloped in the discussion of fees and charges and additional support to aid the carrier's commercial success there. Turizm Ekonomi suggested that marketing support did not materialize to the agreed extent.

    In a recent development, turkey was never a notable part of the ULCC's map. In the all-notable August 2026, for example, only 10 weekly departures existed: six to Dalaman and four to Bodrum. It was the least-served nation in Ryanair's entire network. Only Western Sahara had fewer flights (two), but it is not usually recognized as an independent country.

    Turkey was always a special case for Ryanair because the country does not have an open skies agreement with the EU and the UK. As such, the ULCC's growth was limited. This is why it only flew from Dublin (using its Irish air operator's certificate, with the FR IATA code) and the UK (using Ryanair UK; RK code). The Slovak capital of Bratislava was a special case and was served using a bilateral loophole.

    According to recent reports, think Serbia, think Air Serbia and Wizz Air, not Ryanair. In the peak summer of 2026, Ryanair only had 11 departures to the country, which meant that it was the airline's second least-served nation after Turkey. It had only ever flown to Niš, which is the third most populous administrative area in the country.

    Given the ten-year existence, Niš must have performed sufficiently well overall. According to EX-YU Aviation News, the removal of Nis was due to refueling and fuel regulatory problems. The same source indicates that Ryanair has ruled out flying to Belgrade due to its high costs, although this could change. This is the main reason why it does not fly to the capitals of various other countries in the Balkans.

    Ryanair appears reasonably keen to fly to Belgrade, subject to the right deal. In 2024, the carrier stated that "Belgrade Airport is too expensive and is not an option for us at the moment. We continue to track the [Serbian] market. It is interesting to us. If we can turn potential into a profit, we will." That was before the carrier pulled out of Serbia completely.

    Recent findings suggest that populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising. While populist agendas can come in many different varieties, they are all propelled by a broad sense that the people — or more properly, The People — are being held back by some elite force, whether that be Big Business or an insular political establishment or something darker. If only we can overcome the enemy, we are told, we will sweep to victory on the broad, sunny uplands.

    It has been revealed that as I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared. And so it goes from there, because populism always sooner or later must decide to cling to its narratives when forced to choose between them and empirical reality:.

    Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

    The House has a newly introduced lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a newly introduced challenge: Attendance.
    • Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, remarked attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a newly introduced challenge: Attendance.

    Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-highlights – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    Industry observers note that of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-highlights; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    Recent findings suggest that “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, mentioned. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan mentioned. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., noted. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

    America’s leading natural gas competitor is on track to become its biggest customer. With traffic down through the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar is betting on U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG). The state’s energy organization, QatarEnergy, signed two purchase agreements for American LNG in late October and is reportedly in talks with U.S. supplier Venture Global for a third. There may yet be more deals coming down the pike, including one with Houston-based NextDecade. QatarEnergy already owns 70 percent of Golden Pass LNG, a joint venture with ExxonMobil that shipped its first cargo out of Sabine Pass, Texas, in April.

    Industry observers note that doha’s ventures are adding up. So much so that, according to an early November Financial Times report, Qatar may become “the biggest U.S. LNG buyer” by 2033. This presents the United States with opportunities to affirm market leadership and drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.
